ev.may_g_star_war_562.title: Tikal’s defeat
ev.may_g_star_war_562.text: Caracol, an ally of the Snake kingdom, has crushed Tikal’s army. They say the holy lord Wak Chan K’awiil is dead, and the enemy is smashing statues and stelae in the plazas. Silence and smoke hang over the city.
ev.may_g_star_war_562.defend.success: Your district held, but the victory belongs to the enemy all the same.
ev.may_g_star_war_562.defend.failure: You were badly wounded in the fighting by the palace.
ev.may_g_star_war_562.note: In 562 Caracol, probably backed by Calakmul, defeated Tikal - the "star war" is recorded on Caracol Altar 21. Tikal entered its "hiatus": for almost 130 years the city raised no dated stelae.
ev.may_g_hiatus.title: The years of silence
ev.may_g_hiatus.text: No new stelae have been raised in Tikal’s plazas for a long time. Part of the tribute goes to the enemy, and the old people remember the days when the whole world paid Tikal, not the other way round.
ev.may_g_hiatus.note: After 562 Tikal has almost no dated monuments until 692 - the period is called the "hiatus". The city kept living and building, but it was weakened and surrounded by Calakmul’s allies.
ev.may_g_flight_657.title: The king flees
ev.may_g_flight_657.text: Calakmul’s army, led by Yuknoom Ch’een, has reached Tikal. The lord Nuun Ujol Chaak has fled the city with his retinue. Foreign warriors stand in the plaza, and the enemy’s scribes are already counting the tribute.
ev.may_g_flight_657.note: Dos Pilas inscriptions report that in 657 Yuknoom Ch’een the Great of Calakmul "drove out" Nuun Ujol Chaak from Tikal. Later he accepted Calakmul’s overlordship, and in 659 he was a guest at Palenque.
ev.may_g_dos_pilas_war.title: A war of brothers
ev.may_g_dos_pilas_war.text: Tikal is at war with Dos Pilas, ruled by B’alaj Chan K’awiil - a kinsman of Tikal’s kings who went over to Calakmul. The same blood, the same emblem glyph, and still a war.
ev.may_g_dos_pilas_war.go.success: You came back alive, with spoils and stories.
ev.may_g_dos_pilas_war.go.failure: Tikal’s army was routed. You came back badly wounded.
ev.may_g_dos_pilas_war.home: Give part of the harvest to the war
ev.may_g_dos_pilas_war.note: Dos Pilas was founded in the 640s by B’alaj Chan K’awiil, probably a brother of Tikal’s king. He became Calakmul’s vassal; in 672 Tikal drove him out, but he returned in 677 and in 679 defeated Nuun Ujol Chaak. All this is recorded on the Dos Pilas Hieroglyphic Stairway.
ev.may_g_jasaw.title: A new lord
ev.may_g_jasaw.text: Jasaw Chan K’awiil has taken the throne of Tikal. He is young and, people say, has sworn to restore the city’s glory. In the plaza there are dances, incense and hopes.
ev.may_g_jasaw.note: Jasaw Chan K’awiil I acceded at Tikal in 682 and ruled for about fifty years. Under him the city emerged from the "hiatus" and became a great power again.
ev.may_g_stela30.title: A stela after the silence
ev.may_g_stela30.text: For the k’atun ending Jasaw Chan K’awiil raised a new stela in the plaza - the first in a hundred and thirty years. People touch the carved stone as if to check that it is real.
ev.may_g_stela30.note: Tikal Stela 30 marks the k’atun ending 9.13.0.0.0 (692) - the city’s first dated monument after the hiatus. Jasaw also built a new "twin-pyramid complex" for the k’atun celebration.
ev.may_g_victory_695.title: Victory over the Snake
ev.may_g_victory_695.text: Jasaw’s army has defeated the forces of Calakmul and Yich’aak K’ahk’! The enemy’s palanquin with a giant figure of its patron god has been captured, and noble captives are led through the city. Tikal rejoices for the first time in a century.
ev.may_g_victory_695.note: In 695 Jasaw Chan K’awiil defeated Yich’aak K’ahk’ of Calakmul. The victory is commemorated on the wooden lintels of Temple I, which show the captured enemy palanquin. Calakmul’s hegemony declined afterwards.
ev.may_g_temple_i.title: A temple over the tomb
ev.may_g_temple_i.text: Great Jasaw is dead. Above his tomb on the Great Plaza a steep pyramid is rising - nine terraces, like the nine levels of the underworld. Thousands of hands are needed.
ev.may_g_temple_i.note: Temple I (the "Temple of the Great Jaguar") was raised over the tomb of Jasaw Chan K’awiil, who died around 734, probably under his son Yik’in Chan K’awiil. The tomb held jade, pearls and finely incised bones.
ev.may_g_yikin_wars.title: Yik’in’s victories
ev.may_g_yikin_wars.text: The lord Yik’in Chan K’awiil has defeated Waka’ and Naranjo, Calakmul’s allies, one after the other. Tribute flows into Tikal, and cacao is cheap at the market again.
ev.may_g_yikin_wars.note: In 743 Yik’in Chan K’awiil defeated Waka’ (El Perú), and in 744 Naranjo. The lintels of Temple IV show the captured palanquins of these cities. Tikal became the strongest city in the central lowlands.
ev.may_g_temple_iv.title: The tallest temple
ev.may_g_temple_iv.text: In the west of the city Temple IV is rising - so tall that from the top you can see the forest canopy to the horizon. You hauled lime and stone along with hundreds of others.
ev.may_g_temple_iv.note: Temple IV, about 65 m high, is Tikal’s tallest structure. It is associated with Yik’in Chan K’awiil; a wooden lintel is dated 741.
ev.may_g_tikal_late.title: The city weakens
ev.may_g_tikal_late.text: Tikal is not what it was: subject towns raise stelae to their own kings, tribute fails to arrive, and the population is thinning. Noble families divide the palaces among themselves.
ev.may_g_tikal_late.note: In the early 9th century Tikal’s power fragmented: former subject centres (Ixlu, Jimbal and others) raised stelae of their own. The city’s population fell sharply by the end of the century.
ev.may_g_last_stela_869.title: The last stela
ev.may_g_last_stela_869.text: The lord Jasaw Chan K’awiil II raised a stela for the k’atun ending. The plaza is barely half full, and few believe this is the start of glorious new years.
ev.may_g_last_stela_869.note: Tikal Stela 11 (10.2.0.0.0, 869) is the city’s last dated monument. It was raised by a ruler who took the name of great Jasaw. After that royal power at Tikal faded away.
ev.may_g_tikal_abandon.title: Tikal deserted
ev.may_g_tikal_abandon.text: Ordinary families live in the royal palaces, with hearths burning right in the grand halls. Rubbish piles up by the temple stairs, and the forest is creeping onto the plazas.
ev.may_g_tikal_abandon.note: By the late 9th and 10th centuries Tikal was nearly empty. Archaeologists find traces of the last inhabitants, who squatted in former palaces and left rubbish by the temples. The city was abandoned in the 10th century.
ev.may_g_kaan_arrives.title: The Snake comes to Calakmul
ev.may_g_kaan_arrives.text: The royal Snake dynasty, Kaanul, has firmly settled in Calakmul. The city fills with lords, scribes and craftsmen, and everyone says the world will now be ruled from here.
ev.may_g_kaan_arrives.note: Early monuments of the Snake dynasty are found at Dzibanche. Many scholars believe its capital moved to Calakmul in the 630s, but this is debated.
ev.may_g_yuknoom_great.title: The age of Yuknoom Ch’een
ev.may_g_yuknoom_great.text: Under Yuknoom Ch’een the Great envoys come to Calakmul from all over the lowlands: from Cancuén, Dos Pilas, Naranjo, Waka’. The lord seats kings on their thrones, and tribute - jade, feathers, cacao - flows like a river.
ev.may_g_yuknoom_great.note: Yuknoom Ch’een II (ruled 636–686) was Calakmul’s most powerful king. Inscriptions in many cities say their rulers took the throne "under the supervision" of the Snake lord.
ev.may_g_kaan_palenque.title: A campaign to the west
ev.may_g_kaan_palenque.text: The Snake lord is sending an army far to the west, to Lakamha - the city later called Palenque. It is a long road through rivers and swamps, but rich spoils are promised.
ev.may_g_kaan_palenque.go.success: The enemy city was sacked, and you came back with spoils.
ev.may_g_kaan_palenque.go.failure: Swamp fever struck you down on the way back.
ev.may_g_kaan_palenque.note: Palenque inscriptions record the sacking of the city by Calakmul’s forces in 599 and 611. The campaigns covered hundreds of kilometres - a sign of how far the Snake kingdom’s power reached.
ev.may_g_kaan_defeat.title: Defeat at Tikal
ev.may_g_kaan_defeat.text: Bad news: Calakmul’s army has been beaten by Tikal, and the sacred palanquin bearing the city’s patron has been captured. The lord Yich’aak K’ahk’ no longer appears in the plaza.
ev.may_g_kaan_defeat.note: In 695 Jasaw Chan K’awiil of Tikal defeated Yich’aak K’ahk’. A tomb that may belong to this king, with a jade mask, was found in Calakmul’s Structure II.
ev.may_g_stelae_731.title: A forest of stelae
ev.may_g_stelae_731.text: For the k’atun ending Yuknoom Took’ K’awiil is raising several stelae at once by the Great Pyramid. The city celebrates again as if there had never been a defeat.
ev.may_g_stelae_731.note: In 731 (9.15.0.0.0) Calakmul raised several stelae, among them Stela 51, one of the best preserved. Over 115 stelae have been found at Calakmul - more than at any other Maya city.
ev.may_g_quirigua_plot.title: An embassy to the south
ev.may_g_quirigua_plot.text: The court whispers: the Snake lord has sent an embassy to Quiriguá, far to the south, a vassal of Copán. They say something is being prepared there against Copán’s king.
ev.may_g_quirigua_plot.note: A Quiriguá stela mentions a visit by Wamaaw K’awiil of Calakmul in 736. Many scholars think Calakmul backed Quiriguá’s revolt against Copán in 738, but there is no direct proof.
ev.may_g_calakmul_decline.title: A snake without venom
ev.may_g_calakmul_decline.text: The bajos no longer flood as they used to, and the reservoirs are drying up. The Snake emblem has almost vanished from the inscriptions: Calakmul’s lords now bear a different title and far fewer subjects.
ev.may_g_calakmul_decline.note: After the 730s the Snake emblem at Calakmul gives way to a "Bat" emblem. In the 9th century the city rapidly lost population; late stelae were raised until the early 10th century.
ev.may_g_palenque_sacked.title: Enemies in Lakamha
ev.may_g_palenque_sacked.text: The Snake army came from the east and burst into the city. The shrines of the patron gods have been ransacked, and the priests despair: "The gods are lost; the lord could not protect them."
ev.may_g_palenque_sacked.note: Calakmul sacked Palenque in 599 and 611. Later texts say that afterwards the gods were "lost" and the rites were not performed - a heavy blow to royal authority.
ev.may_g_pakal_accession.title: A twelve-year-old king
ev.may_g_pakal_accession.text: A boy has been placed on the throne of Lakamha - K’inich Janaab Pakal. He is twelve, and at first his mother, Lady Sak K’uk’, rules in his place. People argue whether the city will hold.
ev.may_g_pakal_accession.note: Pakal was born in 603 and took the throne in 615 at the age of twelve; his mother Sak K’uk’ had herself ruled in 612–615. He reigned for 68 years, until 683.
ev.may_g_pakal_palace.title: The White House
ev.may_g_pakal_palace.text: Pakal is rebuilding the palace: new galleries, inner courtyards, stucco reliefs, and on the stairway the figures of captives taken in recent wars. There is work for every craftsman in the city.
ev.may_g_pakal_palace.note: In 654 House E of the Palenque palace, the "White House" where Pakal’s throne stood, was dedicated. In 659 Pakal captured several enemy lords; their images adorn the East Court.
ev.may_g_pakal_death.title: Pakal’s death
ev.may_g_pakal_death.text: K’inich Janaab Pakal, who ruled for almost seventy years, has died. He was laid in a huge stone sarcophagus deep beneath the Temple of the Inscriptions, wearing a jade mask. A stone duct runs up from the tomb so that the king’s spirit can speak with the living.
ev.may_g_pakal_death.note: Pakal died in 683. His tomb beneath the Temple of the Inscriptions, with its carved sarcophagus lid and jade mask, is one of the greatest finds in the Americas (discovered in 1952). The temple was completed by his son K’inich Kan Bahlam II.
ev.may_g_cross_group.title: The Cross temples
ev.may_g_cross_group.text: K’inich Kan Bahlam has dedicated three new temples to the city’s three patron gods. In their sanctuaries stand stone panels telling the history of the world from creation to the present day.
ev.may_g_cross_group.note: The Cross Group (the temples of the Cross, the Foliated Cross and the Sun) was dedicated in 690. Its inscriptions link Palenque’s kings to the patron gods and to mythical events thousands of years earlier.
ev.may_g_tonina_711.title: The king in captivity
ev.may_g_tonina_711.text: Terrible news from the mountains: the lord K’inich K’an Joy Chitam has been captured by the warriors of Toniná. The city is without a king, and the lords argue over who will rule.
ev.may_g_tonina_711.note: In 711 K’an Joy Chitam II, Pakal’s son, was captured by Toniná; a Toniná monument shows him bound. He apparently later returned to Palenque, though this is debated.
ev.may_g_palenque_end.title: The fading of Lakamha
ev.may_g_palenque_end.text: No new inscriptions have been carved in the palace for years. Noble families are moving down to the river, the workshops are closed, and the wind blows through the palace galleries.
ev.may_g_palenque_end.leave: Move to a town by the river
ev.may_g_palenque_end.note: Palenque’s last date is 799 (the accession of Janaab Pakal III, on a ceramic vessel). During the 9th century the city gradually emptied.
ev.may_g_smoke_imix.title: Stelae across the valley
ev.may_g_smoke_imix.text: For the k’atun ending the lord K’ahk’ Uti’ Witz’ K’awiil raised stelae not only in the plaza but throughout the valley - at its edges, as if marking the borders of his world.
ev.may_g_smoke_imix.note: In 652 (9.11.0.0.0) Copán’s twelfth king, "Smoke Imix" (ruled 628–695), set up stelae throughout the valley. His 67-year reign was a time of prosperity for Copán.
ev.may_g_rabbit_738.title: The fall of 18-Rabbit
ev.may_g_rabbit_738.text: The unthinkable: Quiriguá, a small vassal town, has rebelled, and its lord has captured Waxaklajuun Ub’aah K’awiil himself. Within days Copán’s king was dead. The city that raised the finest stelae in the world has fallen silent.
ev.may_g_rabbit_738.note: In 738 K’ahk’ Tiliw Chan Yopaat of Quiriguá captured and executed Copán’s thirteenth king, known as "18-Rabbit". Only months earlier, in January 738, he had dedicated a new ballcourt.
ev.may_g_stairway_755.title: The stairway of glyphs
ev.may_g_stairway_755.text: The lord K’ahk’ Yipyaj Chan K’awiil is completing a temple stairway: every step carries glyphs telling the history of Copán’s kings from the founder on. Two thousand signs - the longest text in the Maya world.
ev.may_g_stairway_755.note: Copán’s Hieroglyphic Stairway (Temple 26) was dedicated in 755. Its more than sixty steps bear about 2,200 glyphs. It restored the city’s pride after the fall of "18-Rabbit".
ev.may_g_altar_q.title: Sixteen kings
ev.may_g_altar_q.text: Yax Pasaj Chan Yopaat has dedicated a square altar: around its sides sit the sixteen lords of Copán, and the first, the founder, hands the staff of power to him, the sixteenth.
ev.may_g_altar_q.note: Altar Q (776) shows the 16 kings of the dynasty, from the founder Yax K’uk’ Mo’ (426) to Yax Pasaj. It is one of the key sources for the history of Copán.
ev.may_g_copan_crowded.title: A crowded valley
ev.may_g_copan_crowded.text: There are so many people in the Copán valley that fields have climbed the steepest slopes. Hardly any forest is left, the downpours wash the soil away, and illnesses of hunger spread among the children.
ev.may_g_copan_crowded.note: By the late 8th century an estimated 20,000–25,000 people lived in the Copán valley. Studies show deforestation, slope erosion and signs of malnutrition in skeletons of the period.
ev.may_g_altar_l.title: The unfinished altar
ev.may_g_altar_l.text: A new claimant, Ukit Took’, ordered an altar to mark his accession. The carvers began one side - and stopped. The stone still stands half blank, like the royal court itself.
ev.may_g_altar_l.note: Copán Altar L (822) was left unfinished - the city’s last royal monument. The dynasty, which had ruled for almost 400 years, came to an end; the valley’s population declined for two more centuries.
ev.may_g_drought.title: The great drought
ev.may_g_drought.text: Year after year the rains are meagre. The reservoirs crack in the sun, and the maize withers as soon as it sprouts. People eat roots and the seeds of the ramón, the breadnut tree that used to feed only peccaries.
ev.may_g_drought.pray: Bring your last gifts to the gods
ev.may_g_drought.note: Lake sediments in Yucatán and cave stalagmites show several severe droughts in the 9th and early 10th centuries. How far drought itself caused the cities’ decline is debated: wars and exhausted land also played a part.
ev.may_g_war_everywhere.title: A time of walls
ev.may_g_war_everywhere.text: Wars are no longer for tribute but for survival: cities surround themselves with palisades and stone walls, fields are burned, and whole villages are carried off. No one remembers when things were last at peace.
ev.may_g_war_everywhere.note: In the late 8th and 9th centuries warfare in the Maya lowlands intensified; hastily built defensive walls have been found at Dos Pilas, Aguateca and other cities. Aguateca was burned by enemies around 810.
ev.may_g_tonina_909.title: The last count
ev.may_g_tonina_909.text: Traders from the west say that in mountain Toniná a monument has been raised bearing a Long Count date. The old people are amazed: in the cities around here no one has carved such dates for a long time.
ev.may_g_tonina_909.note: Toniná Monument 101 bears the date 10.4.0.0.0 (909) - the last known Long Count date in the Maya lowlands. After that the Classic tradition of royal stelae came to an end.
